title: The spider and the web
hookLine: how does one imperishable thing become a whole world? the Mundaka answers with three pictures from any backyard
carry: brahman spins the world from itself
tomorrow: if the rites are true, why call them leaky boats?

lines: A WEB THAT WASN'T THERE LAST NIGHT.
cards: Early morning in a garden. Between two branches hangs a web that wasn't there last night, wet with dew, every thread catching light. And near the middle sits its maker, who brought no materials.
No wood, no wire, no thread from a store. The whole thing came out of the spider's own body. Angiras has just named the imperishable.
The obvious next question: how could one changeless thing turn into everything we see? Instead of a theory, the Mundaka gives three pictures. The first is that spider.

teach.h: AS A SPIDER SPINS AND DRAWS BACK.
teach.b: Here's the verse. Yathorna-nabhih srijate grihnate cha. As a spider sends out its thread and draws it back in.

teach.h: AS PLANTS RISE FROM THE EARTH.
teach.b: As plants spring up from the earth. As hair grows on the head and body of a living person. So, from the imperishable, everything here comes into being.
Each picture teaches something different. The spider: the world doesn't come from some second stuff outside the source. The web is spun from the spider itself, and it can be drawn back in.
The plants: the world rises naturally, the way green comes up after rain, without anybody pushing.
And the hair grows from a living person without that person thinking about it at all. You don't decide to grow your eyebrows. So the source isn't straining.

teach.h: SO, FROM THE IMPERISHABLE, ALL THIS.
teach.b: Then the next verses add: through tapas, that focused heat, Brahman swells, and from it comes food; from food, breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and in action, the deathless.
And the one who knows all, whose very tapas is made of knowledge, gives rise to name, form and food.
That's the teaching: for most schools of Vedanta, Brahman is both the maker of the world and its very stuff, the way the web comes out of the spider. Teachers read the spider differently.
Advaita teachers say the web is an appearance, and the spider alone is ultimately real. Ramanuja's school reads the world as truly Brahman's own body, real and dependent.
Madhva's school reads Brahman as the independent cause of a world that stays distinct from it. All three keep the spider.
Even the Sanskrit word is a small picture: urnanabhi, spider, joins urna, thread or wool, and nabhi, navel.

how: The spider verse of Mundaka 1.1.7 is a standard teaching text in Vedanta, and teachers of different schools explain it in class to show how they understand the relation between Brahman and the world.

games.q: you need to explain how one changeless source becomes a whole world, to a student, in one verse. what do you use?
o: a potter shaping clay he bought.
a spider, plants from the earth, and hair on a body.
a battle between gods and demons.
games.why: the Mundaka uses three pictures: a spider spinning from itself, plants rising, hair growing, and says so from the imperishable comes all this.

practice: Feel your breath go out like a thread and come back in: that's the spider.

Notice what grows in you without effort, your hair, your nails, the steady heartbeat, and let thoughts rise and fall on their own, like plants from the ground. Rest at the center, where the thread comes from.

wordCard.voice: Urnanabhi, the spider. The Mundaka's picture of a world spun from its own source, as naturally as plants from the earth and hair from a living body.

orig.note: Sanskrit ūrṇanābhi, spider: ūrṇā, wool or thread, + nābhi, navel. Mundaka 1.1.7.
